Attraction to specific physical contrasts, such as the visual juxtaposition of different skin tones during intimacy or the appreciation of body curves, is a common and normal aspect of human sexual psychology. 
Human attraction is multifaceted, and your preferences can be understood through a few different lenses: 
1. Visual Contrast and Novelty
The human brain is naturally drawn to high visual contrast and variety. The striking visual difference between lighter and darker skin tones can be aesthetically and sexually stimulating for many individuals. In psychology, sexual preference is often driven by what the brain perceives as visually distinct or exciting. 
2. Aesthetic Appreciation of Curves
Attraction to body curves—such as hip-to-waist ratios—is deeply rooted in evolutionary biology and personal taste. Different ethnicities and body types exhibit various physical traits, and finding specific skeletal or fat distribution patterns (like pronounced curves) highly attractive is a very common preference across all demographics. 
3. Personal Conditioning and Taste
Sexual attraction is unique to every individual. It is shaped by a mix of biological drives, personal experiences, media exposure, and individual aesthetic preferences. What you find visually harmonious or exciting is simply a reflection of your personal "sexual blueprint." 
To help understand your preferences better, we could explore a few different angles. If you'd like, let me know: 
  • If you are interested in how evolutionary biology explains attraction to specific body shapes.
  • Whether you want to discuss the impact of media and culture on forming personal dating preferences.
  • If you are looking to navigate these preferences respectfully within the dating world.

The image shows a handwritten orange character against a dark background, which represents め, the Japanese hiragana character for the syllable "me". 
It is written in two strokes: a slightly slanted downward stroke on the left, followed by a longer, sweeping stroke that loops across and curves around to the right. It is visually very similar to the hiragana character ぬ (nu), but crucially lacks the extra small loop/twist at the bottom-right tail.
